## claude.ai Dropbox
# Claude App MCP LLM Boot Instructions

You are the assistant for Dropbox's Claude App MCP server. Your goal is to help users complete Dropbox tasks quickly and correctly while minimizing friction.

## Customer Use Cases

This app is best at helping users do these Dropbox workflows:

- Browse folder contents and paginate through large directories.
- Find files quickly using plain-language search terms and then open files with follow-on tools.
- Inspect file metadata (size, type, timestamps, IDs, sharing context).
- Check signed-in Dropbox identity, team/account context, and namespace-root context.
- Read text content from supported files up to 5 MiB, and provide a usable Dropbox link even when text extraction fails.
- Generate single-use temporary download links when the user explicitly needs direct file download URLs.
- Generate file previews with thumbnail and "open in Dropbox" experiences.
- Create folders in the right destination before saving artifacts.
- Create new text files directly in Dropbox.
- Create share links for files/folders and return the effective sharing settings.
- Inspect and list existing shared links.
- List, inspect, and create Dropbox file requests.
- Move, rename, copy, and delete Dropbox files/folders after explicit confirmation.
- Check the status of long-running move, copy, and delete jobs.

When users ask "what can you do?", summarize these use cases in plain language before taking action.

## Not Supported (Do Not Advertise)

- Editing or overwriting existing file content in place.
- Saving URL-hosted files directly into Dropbox.
- Uploading local/binary artifacts via `upload_file`.
- Permanent file deletion or wipe workflows. `delete` moves items to the user's Dropbox "Deleted files" area only.
- Reliable text extraction for supported files via `fetch`; extraction may still fail for some files, in which case the tool error may include a usable link.
- E-signature initiation or signing workflows.
- Actions outside Dropbox content management and sharing.

## devonthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. (2) Output protection: result lists from tools like search_records, classify_record, find_similar_records, get_record_children, get_record_duplicates, and the link traversal tools are filt… [truncated]

## omnifocus
OmniFocus is a GTD task manager. Hierarchy: Folders > Projects > Tasks > Subtasks.

TASK STATES: Available, Blocked, Deferred (future defer date), Flagged, Overdue, Completed, Dropped. Planned Date is a scheduling signal only — no availability/overdue constraints.

PROJECT TYPES: "sequential" (tasks in order; first incomplete = available, rest blocked; position = dependencies), "parallel" (all available), "single_actions" (no completion goal, cannot auto-complete). The `next` field is true for the first available action in a sequential project/action group; in parallel projects, all incomplete tasks have `next: true`.

ACTION GROUPS: Task with subtasks. Parent shows `blocked: true` while subtasks are active — this is normal, not an error. Do not try to unblock it.

INHERITED STATUS: `completed`/`dropped` reflect the task's own state, not its container's. `effectivelyCompleted`/`effectivelyDropped` reflect the container's state — if true, the task's parent project or action group was completed/dropped. Task in completed project: `completed: false`, `effectivelyCompleted: true`, `available: false`. Use `available_only=True` for actionable tasks.

EFFECTIVE DATES: Dates returned by get_tasks are always effective (inherited). A task with no direct due date WILL show its project's due date in the dueDate field — this is correct behavior, not a bug. You cannot clear an inherited date at the task level. Write operations set the task's own date.

RECURRING TASKS: `completed=True` uses `mark complete`, which creates the next occurrence. This is guaranteed. WARNING: Dropping a recurring task (status='dropped') without clearing recurrence first (recurrence='') spawns the next occurrence. To stop a series: update_tasks([{"id": "...", "recurrence": "", "status": "dropped"}]).

TAGS: Represent work contexts. Tag statuses: Active (normal), On Hold (tasks excluded from Available perspective), Dropped (tag hidden from picker; does NOT affect task availability).

DEFER vs DUE: Defer = hidden until that date. Due = deadline.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/marklevison/.claude/skills/domain-modeling

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline — challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `CONTEXT.md` for vocabulary is not this skill — that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── CONTEXT.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `CONTEXT-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── CONTEXT-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── CONTEXT.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── CONTEXT.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily — only when you have something to write. If no `CONTEXT.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `CONTEXT.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y — which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account' — do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible — which is right?"

### Update CONTEXT.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `CONTEXT.md` right there. Don't batch these up — capture them as they happen. Use the format in [CONTEXT-FORMAT.md](./CONTEXT-FORMAT.md).

`CONTEXT.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `CONTEXT.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse** — the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context** — a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off** — there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

- **Resize on upload already ships.** `ReceiptService.prepareFileForUpload()` (`src/lib/services/ReceiptService.ts:201`) calls `resizeImage(file, 2000, 0.85)` — Canvas, longest axis 2000px, JPEG 85%, EXIF-corrected via `createImageBitmap`, falls back to the original on any error. Commit `901b670` "Resize images on upload".
- **Zoom already ships.** `ReceiptImageViewer.svelte` — wheel/pinch/double-tap zoom anchored to cursor, drag-to-scroll, keyboard parity, `MIN_ZOOM 100` → `MAX_ZOOM 400`, 50% steps.
- **JPEG/PNG only.** `imageResize.ts:72` returns the file untouched for anything else — including `image/heic`, which the receipts `accept` list permits. Already logged in the backlog (line 20) as a suspected iOS bug.
- **A one-off bulk re-resizer exists**: `/admin/resize-images`, client-only, no authz beyond `confirm()` (backlog M2).

One fact that matters for everything below: 100% zoom means *fit-to-viewport*, not 1:1 pixels (`handleImageLoad`, `ReceiptImageViewer.svelte:72`). On a laptop a receipt fits at ~800px tall, so 400% asks for ~3200px of detail from a 2000px source — past that point you're magnifying interpolation, not revealing text. The zoom ceiling and the resize target are the same decision seen from two ends.

So my first question is about what actually prompted this.

content.text:
Found it. This isn't a resize-quality problem at all — it's an ordering bug.

`uploadAndCreate()` validates **before** it resizes (`ReceiptService.ts:187` → `:191`):

```
validateFile(file)          // ← rejects >5MB   ReceiptService.ts:187
  └─ prepareFileForUpload() // ← resize to 2000px/85%   :191
```

So the 5MB gate (`MAX_IMAGE_MB`, `:13`) measures the file your phone handed over, not the file we actually store. A modern iPhone JPEG runs 3–5MB and a 48MP one 8–12MB; after `resizeImage()` that same receipt lands around 300–600KB. The pipeline is throwing away files it was built to shrink by 10–20×, with the message "Image too large. Max 5MB." — which asks the user to do by hand the exact job the next line of code does automatically.

There's no second gate that saves it: `FileValidator` (`src/lib/server/fileValidation.ts:13`, 10MB, magic-number based) is server-side and isn't on this path, and the email-ingestion path has no size check at all — so the same receipt forwarded by email would sail through while the upload button rejects it.

That makes the first real decision what the size limit is *for*.

questions.question: What should the 5MB limit actually govern?

options.label: Gate what we store (Recommended)
options.description: Move the size check after resize. Anything that shrinks under the limit is accepted, however big it arrived. Keep a high ceiling on the original (~25MB) purely to stop a monster file OOM-ing Canvas on a phone. Fixes the reported failure and the storage-cost concern at once.

options.label: Just raise the image limit
options.description: Bump MAX_IMAGE_MB from 5 to ~15. One-line change, unblocks you today, but the gate still measures the wrong artifact — and a 16MB photo that would resize to 400KB is still refused.

options.label: Keep the gate, fix the message
options.description: Leave behaviour alone; tell the user what to do about it. Cheapest, but keeps a manual step that the code already automates.

content.text:
Next branch: the files that never get resized.

`resizeImage()` returns the file untouched unless it's `image/jpeg` or `image/png` (`imageResize.ts:72`), but the upload `accept` list offers `image/heic` too (`src/routes/receipts/+page.svelte:492`). Under "gate what we store," a HEIC's stored size *is* its original size — so an iPhone HEIC over 5MB would still be rejected, and one under 5MB gets stored and sent to Mistral at full resolution. Given the reported failure was a phone photo, this is likely the path you actually hit.

Relevant: HEIC decoding in Canvas works in Safari (macOS/iOS) but not Chrome or Firefox — and Safari is precisely where HEIC comes from.

options.label: Resize + transcode to JPEG (Recommended)
options.description: Feed HEIC through the same Canvas path but always emit JPEG (filename extension too). Works in Safari where HEIC originates; falls back to the untouched original elsewhere. Also removes any doubt about whether Mistral OCR handles HEIC.

options.label: Leave HEIC unresized
options.description: Keep the 5MB gate applying to HEIC originals. Simplest, but iPhone users keep hitting the exact rejection you reported, and full-res photos go to storage and OCR.

options.label: Stop accepting HEIC
options.description: Drop image/heic from the accept list so iOS is forced to hand over JPEG. Fewer code paths, but risks an outright 'unsupported file type' error if a device offers HEIC anyway.

options.label: Defer — verify on-device first

content.text:
Now the quality end of it — your original brief said "clear and readable, zoom into small bits of text."

The viewer math says the current pair is already mismatched. 100% = fit-to-viewport (`ReceiptImageViewer.svelte:78`). A 2000×900 receipt on a 1440px-tall laptop fits at ~1150px tall, so 100% ≈ 57% of native. `MAX_ZOOM = 400` then asks the browser to paint ~4600px from a 2000px source — a 2.3× upscale. Past roughly 175% zoom, every additional step is interpolation, not detail. That's the mechanism behind mushy text, and it's set by two constants that were chosen independently.

One caveat I can't resolve from here: Mistral's vision model downscales large images internally, so pixels beyond ~1000–1500px on an axis likely do nothing for OCR accuracy. Extra resolution is for human eyes only. Worth verifying against Mistral's docs before treating "better OCR" as a reason to store more.

questions.question: How many pixels should we keep, given zoom-to-read is the goal?

options.label: 2400px @ 85% (Recommended)
options.description: Modest bump for headroom on receipts photographed at a distance. ~500–800KB stored. Pairs with capping zoom near native so the viewer stops promising detail the file doesn't have.

options.label: Keep 2000px @ 85%
options.description: Change nothing about quality — the reported failure was the size gate, not sharpness. Smallest files. Fix the zoom ceiling instead so 400% stops overselling.

options.label: 3000px @ 90%
options.description: Generous — supports real 1:1 inspection of fine print even on a large monitor. ~1–1.5MB stored, roughly 3× today's storage and slower loads on the receipts list.

content.text:
Then the other half of that pair — the zoom ceiling.

With a 2400px source, `MAX_ZOOM = 400` means very different things per device: on a phone (~600px of viewport height) 400% lands almost exactly at native 1:1, but on a desktop it's 2× past native. A flat percentage can't be right on both.

Worth weighing against accessibility: magnifying past 1:1 still helps low-vision readers even though it adds no information, so a hard 1:1 stop would be a small regression for them.

questions.question: How should the zoom ceiling be set?

options.label: Derive from the image, ~1.5× native (Recommended)
options.description: Compute the zoom that equals 1:1 pixels for this image on this screen, allow 50% beyond it for magnification, clamp to a sane range. Device-correct, keeps the low-vision headroom, stops promising 4× detail that isn't there.

options.label: Keep the flat 400%
options.description: No viewer change at all — the extra source pixels from 2400px simply make 400% look better than it does today. Zero risk, but desktop users still hit interpolation near the top of the range.

options.label: Hard stop at 1:1 native
options.description: Never upscale. Maximally honest — every pixel on screen is a real pixel — but removes magnification as an accessibility aid and will feel like the zoom 'ran out' on phones.

Taking that as decided — with one consequence I want on the record, because it silently removes a capability.

`handleImageLoad` clamps the fit scale to a maximum of 1 (`ReceiptImageViewer.svelte:78`), so an image *smaller* than the viewport displays at its natural size and 100% already **is** 1:1. Under a hard native stop, `MIN_ZOOM` and `MAX_ZOOM` collapse to the same value and both zoom buttons go permanently disabled for that receipt. Today those same images zoom to 400%.

This isn't hypothetical: it hits every small PNG, every receipt uploaded before the resize feature landed at low resolution, and — on a desktop — anything under roughly 1300px tall.

content.text:
Two numbers fall out of "gate what we store," and they interact with the fallback path.

`prepareFileForUpload` swallows any resize error and returns the **original** (`ReceiptService.ts:215`). Under the new ordering that changes meaning: a 12MB photo whose resize fails — HEIC in Chrome, a Canvas OOM, a corrupt EXIF block — now falls back to a 12MB original that the post-resize gate rejects. Today that same file is rejected earlier and more bluntly. Either way it fails, but the reason is now "we couldn't shrink it," not "it's too big."

So we need a pre-resize ceiling that exists purely to stop a monster file from wedging the browser before we ever get to Canvas.

questions.question: What should the pre-resize hard ceiling be, before we even attempt to decode?

options.label: 25MB, any type (Recommended)
options.description: Comfortably above a 48MP iPhone photo (~12MB) and a scanned multi-page PDF, low enough to stop a DSLR RAW-export or a 200MP panorama from hanging a phone. Post-resize gate stays 5MB images / 10MB PDF.

options.label: 50MB
options.description: Effectively 'anything a phone or scanner produces'. Fewer false rejections, but a 50MB decode on an older phone can freeze the tab for seconds or crash it outright.

options.label: No pre-resize ceiling
options.description: Attempt the resize on anything and let the post-resize gate decide. Simplest rule to explain, but hands an unbounded decode to Canvas — a bad file becomes a hung tab with no error.

options.label: 10MB
options.description: Conservative. Note this would still reject the 48MP iPhone photos this whole change is meant to accept, so it partly undoes the fix.

One consequence worth stating rather than asking about: **no backfill is needed, and that's a property of the choice you just made.** Storage now holds three generations — full-resolution originals from before `901b670`, 2000px ones since, and 2400px going forward. A zoom ceiling derived from each image's own natural size handles all three correctly on its own: the old full-res receipts simply permit more zoom. Re-resizing them down would destroy detail you already paid to store. So `/admin/resize-images` has no remaining job — which matters, because it's the unauthenticated delete-and-reupload page flagged as **M2** in the backlog.

Let me check the email path before asking the next one.

content.text:
Confirmed — the email path uploads attachment bytes straight to storage (`handler.ts:137`) with no size check and no resize. It's a Deno edge function, so there's no Canvas; shrinking there means pulling in a WASM image library and duplicating the resize rules in `supabase/functions/_shared/` (the same lock-step maintenance burden CLAUDE.md already flags for the date-correction code).

So a receipt emailed in is stored at full phone resolution, while the same receipt uploaded through the browser becomes 2400px.

content.text: Two defects surfaced while tracing the resize path, one of which is a real decision. **PNG is never compressed.** `canvas.toBlob(cb, file.type, quality)` (`imageResize.ts:104`) — the quality argument is ignored for `image/png` because PNG is lossless. So the 85% never applies, and the doc comment at `imageResize.ts:58` ("Images smaller than 2000px still have compression applied") is false for PNG. Worse, there's no "keep whichever is smaller" check: a sub-2400px PNG gets re-encoded at identical dimensions and the result is returned even when it's *larger* than what the user picked. Screenshots of e-receipts are usually PNG, so this is a common path. **The file is decoded twice.** `resizeImage` creates an `` from an object URL purely to get an `onload`, then ignores it and calls `createImageBitmap(file)` to decode the same bytes again (`imageResize.ts:77` vs `:89`). Peak memory is doubled on exactly the large files the 25MB ceiling now admits — on a phone that's the difference between working and a tab crash. I'd fold removing the redundant decode into this work; it's not a judgment call. The PNG question is a judgment call:

questions.question: How should PNG uploads be handled?

options.label: Transcode PNG to JPEG at 85% (Recommended)
options.description: Same treatment as HEIC — one output format, and 85% actually applies. A photographed or screenshotted receipt is continuous-tone content that JPEG handles well. Loses nothing that matters for a receipt; filename extension changes.

options.label: Keep PNG, add a 'keep the smaller file' guard
options.description: Preserve the format but never return a result bigger than the input. Safest for sharp-edged screenshot text (JPEG ringing around small glyphs is real), though a full-page PNG screenshot stays several MB.

options.label: Transcode only when it wins
options.description: Encode JPEG, compare against the original PNG, keep whichever is smaller. Best size outcome, but the stored format now varies per file — harder to reason about and to test.

1	# YFL Expense Tracker
2	
3	Family expense tracking. Family members capture what they spent — mostly by
4	uploading receipt images, sometimes by typing the details in by hand — and the
5	app derives their expenses and reconciles them against imported bank activity.
6	
7	## Language
8	
9	**Family**:
10	The data-scoping unit. All Receipts, Transactions, Categories, and vendor rules
11	belong to a Family, and every access-control policy scopes to it. Each user gets
12	one solo Family auto-created at signup (`ensure_default_family()`); their
13	`is_default` Family is the one they operate on. A `families` row (`id`, `name`).
14	_Avoid_: household, account
15	
16	**Family Member**:
17	A person who belongs to a Family — a `family_members` row (`family_id`,
18	`user_id`, `role`, `status`, `is_default`). `role ∈ {owner, member}` (the creator
19	is the `owner`; role is not yet used for authorization). `status ∈ {active,
20	invited, removed}`, but only `active` rows exist until Invitations ship. A member
21	is identified for display by their primary email (from `auth.users`), which the
22	client reads only through the `get_family_members()` `SECURITY DEFINER` RPC.
23	_Avoid_: user, member, participant
24	
25	**Receipt**:
26	A record of a single purchase (merchant, amount, date). May originate from an
27	uploaded image or be entered by hand. Each Receipt maps to exactly one Expense.
28	_Avoid_: bill, purchase
29	
30	**Manual Receipt**:
31	A Receipt a person creates by typing merchant, amount, and date rather than
32	uploading an image. It has no image and is not run through OCR; the person is
33	asserting the details — including the date — directly.
34	_Avoid_: manual entry, hand receipt
35	
36	**Expense**:
37	The categorized view of a Receipt used for reporting. Derived one-to-one from a
38	Receipt — never stored on its own. Talk about Expenses when reporting or
39	categorizing; talk about Receipts when capturing.
40	_Avoid_: cost, spend
41	
42	**Area of Importance**:
43	The top tier of the spending hierarchy — e.g. Essential, Priorities, Other. A
44	family-scoped `importance_areas` row with a `sort_order`. Attaches to the
45	**Grouping**, not to individual categories, so a Grouping has exactly one
46	Importance.
47	_Avoid_: priority band, tier
48	
49	**Grouping**:
50	The middle tier of the spending hierarchy — e.g. Everyday, Home, Transportation.
51	A family-scoped `category_groups` row that belongs to one **Area of Importance**
52	and gathers many Categories. A Category with no Grouping is _Uncategorized_.
53	_Avoid_: group, bucket, section
54	
55	**Spending Report**:
56	The categorized roll-up of a year's Expenses through Category → Grouping → Area
57	of Importance, shown as a month-by-month table (the `/spending` "Table" view) or
58	the **Spending Chart**. Replaces the family's hand-built spreadsheet pivot.
59	_Avoid_: pivot table, summary
60	
61	**Spending Chart**:
62	The charted form of the **Spending Report**: stacked bars (one per Grouping,
63	stacked by month) with drilldown to Categories — the `/spending` "Chart" view.
64	_Avoid_: graph, dashboard
65	
66	**Transaction**:
67	A line of activity imported from a bank or credit-card statement, reconciled
68	against Receipts. Distinct from a Receipt: it comes from the bank, not the user.
69	_Avoid_: charge, payment
70	
71	**Split Receipt**:
72	A partial-amount Receipt carved off another. A split is a FULL Receipt record
73	(not a line-item or child), preserving the 1:1 Receipt↔Expense invariant so no
74	query or reconciliation code needs to change. Peers share a nullable, indexed
75	`split_group_id` (UUID). Created by an atomic insert-then-update — the new split
76	is inserted first, the original reduced second; if the update fails the split is
77	deleted (best-effort rollback). Both the original's and the split's
78	`matched_transaction_id` are cleared. Each split takes an optional per-split date
79	override (deferred charges: hotel/AirBnB/installments) and recomputes
80	`suspicious_date` from its own date. Splits share the original
81	`receipt_image_path` — no file is duplicated.
82	_Avoid_: line item, child receipt
83	
84	**Potential Duplicate**:
85	Two or more Receipts that may record the same purchase — a suspicion raised by
86	the app, never an assertion. Always _potential_: a family can legitimately hold
87	two Receipts for the same merchant, amount and day. Duplicate-ness is a property
88	of a **pair** of Receipts, not of one Receipt, and it is derived on demand rather
89	than recorded. There is currently no way for a person to settle the suspicion.
90	_Avoid_: duplicate (unqualified), copy, repeat
91	
92	## Invariants
93	
94	**Family-scoped migration invariants**:
95	When categories and vendor rules moved from user- to family-scope, duplicates
96	were deduped keeping the FIRST-created row per key; the losing rows' receipt
97	categorizations become uncategorized via `expense_categories`
98	`ON DELETE SET NULL`. Category names are unique per family, case-insensitive
99	(`unique_category_per_family` on `(family_id, LOWER(name))`); vendor patterns are
100	unique per `(family_id, vendor_pattern)`. Every family-scoped RLS policy requires
101	`family_members.status = 'active'`. These migrations do not roll back cleanly —
102	fix forward.
103	
104	**Foreign-currency reconciliation**:
105	A Receipt's `total_amount` stays in its ORIGINAL currency; `exchange_rate_to_cad`
106	is stored on the Receipt at save time (fetched once, never during
107	reconciliation). Reconciliation matches CAD receipts within a $0.01 tolerance but
108	foreign-currency receipts within 5% — rate approximation, the ~FX fee, and
109	settlement timing all move the number. Rates come from the Bank of Canada Valet
110	API (series `FXEURCAD`, `FXUSDCAD`, `FXGBPCAD`).
111	
112	**Transaction import dedup**:
113	Count-based so legitimate in-file repeats survive: for each match key it inserts
114	`max(0, fileCount − dbCount)` rows, which makes re-import idempotent. The match
115	key is scoped per family + `credit_card_type`. Excluded rows deliberately count
116	toward the DB total, so re-importing does not resurrect them.
117	
118	**Suspicious-date authority**:
119	Only OCR/automated extraction sets `suspicious_date`. Manual create and any manual
120	date edit always CLEAR it — user intent is authoritative. Saving through the
121	receipt edit modal is the confirmation action; there is no separate "confirm
122	date".
123	
124	**Suspicious-date scope**:
125	A suspicious date is a statement that the Receipt's date is untrustworthy, so
126	that date cannot also be used to decide whether the Receipt is in scope. Counting
127	or filtering flagged Receipts by the date window would hide exactly the ones
128	whose date is wrong — they have been filed into the wrong window. The flag is
129	therefore family-global, deliberately, even while the list beneath it is
130	date-filtered. Contrast **Split Receipt** grouping, where `split_group_id` is a
131	trustworthy stored fact and can be resolved globally with no such tension.
132	
133	**Receipt minimum-data rule**:
134	A Receipt may be saved with empty fields, but at least ONE of merchant / amount /
135	date must be non-empty.
136	
137	**Expense categorization precedence**:
138	Manual category assignments are never overwritten by auto (vendor-rule)
139	assignments — auto-categorization only touches uncategorized expenses. New
140	families get 43 default categories.

`receipt_image_path` — no file is duplicated.
_Avoid_: line item, child receipt

**Potential Duplicate**:
Two or more Receipts that may record the same purchase — a suspicion raised by
the app, never an assertion. Always _potential_: a family can legitimately hold
two Receipts for the same merchant, amount and day. Duplicate-ness is a property
of a **pair** of Receipts, not of one Receipt, and it is derived on demand rather
than recorded. There is currently no way for a person to settle the suspicion.
_Avoid_: duplicate (unqualified), copy, repeat

## Invariants

**Family-scoped migration invariants**:
When categories and vendor rules moved from user- to family-scope, duplicates
were deduped keeping the FIRST-created row per key; the losing rows' receipt
categorizations become uncategorized via `expense_categories`
`ON DELETE SET NULL`. Category names are unique per family, case-insensitive
(`unique_category_per_family` on `(family_id, LOWER(name))`); vendor patterns are
unique per `(family_id, vendor_pattern)`. Every family-scoped RLS policy requires
`family_members.status = 'active'`. These migrations do not roll back cleanly —
fix forward.

**Foreign-currency reconciliation**:
A Receipt's `total_amount` stays in its ORIGINAL currency; `exchange_rate_to_cad`
is stored on the Receipt at save time (fetched once, never during
reconciliation). Reconciliation matches CAD receipts within a $0.01 tolerance but
foreign-currency receipts within 5% — rate approximation, the ~FX fee, and
settlement timing all move the number. Rates come from the Bank of Canada Valet
API (series `FXEURCAD`, `FXUSDCAD`, `FXGBPCAD`).

**Transaction import dedup**:
Count-based so legitimate in-file repeats survive: for each match key it inserts
`max(0, fileCount − dbCount)` rows, which makes re-import idempotent. The match
key is scoped per family + `credit_card_type`. Excluded rows deliberately count
toward the DB total, so re-importing does not resurrect them.

**Suspicious-date authority**:
Only OCR/automated extraction sets `suspicious_date`. Manual create and any manual
date edit always CLEAR it — user intent is authoritative. Saving through the
receipt edit modal is the confirmation action; there is no separate "confirm
date".

**Suspicious-date scope**:
A suspicious date is a statement that the Receipt's date is untrustworthy, so
that date cannot also be used to decide whether the Receipt is in scope. Counting
or filtering flagged Receipts by the date window would hide exactly the ones
whose date is wrong — they have been filed into the wrong window. The flag is
therefore family-global, deliberately, even while the list beneath it is
date-filtered. Contrast **Split Receipt** grouping, where `split_group_id` is a
trustworthy stored fact and can be resolved globally with no such tension.

**Receipt minimum-data rule**:
A Receipt may be saved with empty fields, but at least ONE of merchant / amount /
date must be non-empty.

**Expense categorization precedence**:
Manual category assignments are never overwritten by auto (vendor-rule)
assignments — auto-categorization only touches uncategorized expenses. New
families get 43 default categories.

Vocabulary. The glossary in `docs/domain-model.md` has no word for the artifact this whole change is about, and the ambiguity is exactly what produced the bug: `validateFile` measured one thing while the limit was meant to describe another. Two terms would have made the ordering error visible.

I'd propose adding to **Language**:

- **Source File** — what a person hands the app: a camera photo, a screenshot, a HEIC from Photos, an emailed attachment. Transient; discarded after upload. Only its name survives, in `original_filename`. _Avoid_: upload, original, the image
- **Receipt Image** — the single JPEG we derive and store for a Receipt, at `receipt_image_path`. Never the Source File. A PDF receipt is stored unmodified and is not a Receipt Image. _Avoid_: photo, scan, original, attachment

and to **Invariants**:

- **Size limits govern the Receipt Image** — the 5MB/10MB limits state what we agree to *store*. The Source File is bounded only by a decode guard, because asking a person to shrink a photo duplicates work the code does one line later.
- **Zoom never invents pixels** — 100% is fit-to-viewport; the ceiling is the image's own natural resolution. Zoom therefore disables itself for images at or below viewport size, and the three storage generations (pre-`901b670` full-res, 2000px, 2400px) each get a correct ceiling with no migration.
- **Every uploaded image becomes JPEG** — HEIC and PNG transcode; only PDFs pass through untouched. Resize is browser-only, so emailed receipts are stored as received.

Nothing written yet — confirm and I'll produce the three docs. ## The actual defect `uploadAndCreate()` validates the file the person picked, then shrinks it (`ReceiptService.ts:187` → `:191`). The 5MB gate measures the wrong artifact, so a phone photo is rejected with "Image too large. Max 5MB." one line before the code that would have made it ~400KB. That's the "too big" you hit last month. ## Decisions | | | |---|---| | **Gate** | Moves after resize — the limit describes the **Receipt Image** we store, not the **Source File**. 25MB pre-decode ceiling on any type, purely to stop a monster file wedging the browser. Post-resize: 5MB images / 10MB PDF. | | **Pixels** | 2400px longest axis @ 85% (up from 2000px). | | **Formats** | HEIC and PNG both transcode to JPEG. Every stored image is a JPEG; only PDFs pass through untouched. `original_filename` keeps the name the person recognizes (`#{#ofn2a}`). | | **Zoom** | Hard stop at 1:1 native — derived per image, replacing the flat `MAX_ZOOM = 400`. Zoom disables itself when an image is already at or under viewport size; that's accepted as the honest outcome. | | **Backfill** | None. Each generation gets a correct ceiling from its own natural size. | | **`/admin/resize-images`** | Deleted — job done, and it would now destroy detail. Closes backlog **M2**. | | **Email path** | Unchanged; asymmetry recorded in the domain model plus a backlog item (from your earlier answer). | ## Rolled in as consequences, not separate choices - **`extractReceiptDataFailSoft(path, file.type)` (`:193`) must pass the *uploaded* file's type.** Transcoding makes this a live bug: OCR would be told `image/heic` about a JPEG. - **Drop the redundant decode.** `resizeImage` builds an `` from an object URL only to get an `onload`, then decodes the same bytes again via `createImageBitmap` (`imageResize.ts:77`, `:89`). Doubled peak memory on exactly the large files the 25MB ceiling now admits. - **PNG "compression" was never happening.** `toBlob`'s quality argument is ignored for PNG, and a sub-threshold PNG could be returned *larger* than it arrived. Transcoding resolves both; the false comment at `imageResize.ts:58` goes with it. - **Resize sits inside `withRetry` (`:190`)**, so every retry re-decodes from the original. Idempotent, not incorrect — noting it, not changing it. ## Two things I'd verify during implementation, not assume 1. **Whether 2400px buys OCR anything.** Mistral's vision model downscales large inputs internally; if the effective ceiling is ~1024–1500px, the extra pixels serve human zoom only. Worth reading Mistral's docs — it doesn't change the decision, but it changes the *rationale* the ADR records. 2. **What an iPhone actually hands over.** The backlog flags this as never confirmed on-device. The HEIC transcode is designed to work whether Safari hands over HEIC or JPEG, so this is a validation step, not a blocker. # ADR Format

ADRs live in `docs/adr/` and use sequential numbering: `0001-slug.md`, `0002-slug.md`, etc.

Create the `docs/adr/` directory lazily — only when the first ADR is needed.

## Template

```md
# {Short title of the decision}

{1-3 sentences: what's the context, what did we decide, and why.}
```

That's it. An ADR can be a single paragraph. The value is in recording *that* a decision was made and *why* — not in filling out sections.

## Optional sections

Only include these when they add genuine value. Most ADRs won't need them.

- **Status** frontmatter (`proposed | accepted | deprecated | superseded by ADR-NNNN`) — useful when decisions are revisited
- **Considered Options** — only when the rejected alternatives are worth remembering
- **Consequences** — only when non-obvious downstream effects need to be called out

## Numbering

Scan `docs/adr/` for the highest existing number and increment by one.

## When to offer an ADR

All three of these must be true:

1. **Hard to reverse** — the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context** — a future reader will look at the code and wonder "why on earth did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off** — there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If a decision is easy to reverse, skip it — you'll just reverse it. If it's not surprising, nobody will wonder why. If there was no real alternative, there's nothing to record beyond "we did the obvious thing."

### What qualifies

- **Architectural shape.** "We're using a monorepo." "The write model is event-sourced, the read model is projected into Postgres."
- **Integration patterns between contexts.** "Ordering and Billing communicate via domain events, not synchronous HTTP."
- **Technology choices that carry lock-in.** Database, message bus, auth provider, deployment target. Not every library — just the ones that would take a quarter to swap out.
- **Boundary and scope decisions.** "Customer data is owned by the Customer context; other contexts reference it by ID only." The explicit no-s are as valuable as the yes-s.
- **Deliberate deviations from the obvious path.** "We're using manual SQL instead of an ORM because X." Anything where a reasonable reader would assume the opposite. These stop the next engineer from "fixing" something that was deliberate.
- **Constraints not visible in the code.** "We can't use AWS because of compliance requirements." "Response times must be under 200ms because of the partner API contract."
- **Rejected alternatives when the rejection is non-obvious.** If you considered GraphQL and picked REST for subtle reasons, record it — otherwise someone will suggest GraphQL again in six months.

42	  Genuinely solves the no-PR problem: it holds a production build off the

44	  merge. Rejected anyway. Deployment Checks has no runner of its own — it only

# Quality gate lives in the Vercel build, not GitHub Actions

## Context & decision

The [type-check-cleanup PRD](../prd-done/prd-type-check-cleanup.md) got
`npm run check` to 0 errors / 0 warnings and left one deliverable open: making
the check a gate so the green state cannot silently regress. The repo had no CI
at all.

The usual answer — a workflow on `pull_request` that blocks the merge — does not
apply here. **This project commits straight to `master` and will never use pull
requests.** There is no merge to block.

The gate therefore lives in `vercel.json`:

```json
"buildCommand": "npm run check && npm run lint && vitest run --project server && npm run build"
```

Vercel already deploys by watching GitHub, so every push runs this. A failure
means the build never succeeds and **no deployment is created** — there is
nothing to promote, accidentally or otherwise. The config is version-controlled
rather than set in the dashboard.

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` remains, reduced to the one suite the Vercel build
image cannot run: the `client` Vitest project needs real Chromium via the
Playwright provider, and `playwright install --with-deps` wants root + apt. That
workflow is **advisory** and gates nothing.

## Considered options

- **GitHub Actions on `pull_request`, blocking merge (the standard answer).**
  Rejected outright: there are no pull requests, so the trigger would never fire.
- **GitHub Actions on `push`, advisory only.** Catches regressions but blocks
  nothing — Vercel promotes the broken build while the workflow is still running.
  Kept only for the browser tests, where advisory is the honest description.
- **[Vercel Deployment Checks](https://vercel.com/docs/deployment-checks).**
  Genuinely solves the no-PR problem: it holds a production build off the
  production domain until a named check passes, gating _release_ rather than
  merge. Rejected anyway. Deployment Checks has no runner of its own — it only
  consumes GitHub Actions results or Marketplace integrations — so it puts
  GitHub Actions squarely in the release path and **fails closed**. An Actions
  outage would leave good builds unpromoted, and the escape hatch is
  `Force Promote`. Reaching for that a few times turns bypassing the gate into
  reflex, which is worse than having no gate. We do not trust Actions enough to
  make shipping depend on it.
- **Gate inside the Vercel build (chosen).** Runs on Vercel's own
  infrastructure, no third party in the release path, no dashboard state, and a
  stronger failure mode than promote-time gating: the artifact never exists.

## Consequences

- Every push spends ~1.5 min on verification before building. Acceptable here;
  revisit if deploy latency starts to hurt.
- A failing check blocks **preview** deployments too, not just production.
- There is no `Force Promote` equivalent. Shipping past a failing lint means
  fixing it or editing `vercel.json` — a sharper edge than promote-time gating,
  and deliberate.
- The browser tests are outside the gate. A regression caught only by the
  `client` project can reach production; GitHub Actions will report it after the
  fact.
- `test:e2e` and `test:integration` need a live Supabase stack and run nowhere
  automatically. Tracked in the [backlog](../product-backlog.md).
- If the gate ever needs to move back to promote-time, note that Vercel matches
  Deployment Checks **by job name** — renaming a job silently detaches the check.

# Spending Report Design

**Date:** 2026-07-09
**Status:** ✅ Built — table + chart views, cell drill-down, hierarchy editing
(assign categories to groups, re-parent groups, add & rename Groupings),
**historical-year expense upload from CSV/Excel**, and **year-over-year
comparison** (a Change column on the table + side-by-side prior-year bars on the
chart) are all shipped and live. A third comparison view — a horizontal **Bridge /
waterfall** — was built and then **abandoned as not intuitive** and **removed**; see
[ADR-0004](../adr/0004-abandon-spending-bridge-waterfall-view.md). Remaining work
is the
[Deferred](#deferred-later-slices) slices (richer YoY views — cumulative pace
line, diverging change bars — plus period selection and export).
Grouping tier editing is built; what's left of "tier CRUD" is deliberately out of
scope (fixed Importance areas, no Grouping delete/reorder).

## Overview

A top-level **Spending** report that rolls up Expenses by **Importance →
Grouping → Category** across the months of a year. It replaces the Excel pivot
table the family currently maintains by hand. ("Spending Report" is the working
term; pin the final ubiquitous-language name in `domain-model.md` when built.)

Built ✅: the **table view** (v1), the **chart view** (an accordion magnitude bar
chart), **cell drill-down** into the Expenses view, and **hierarchy editing**
(assign categories to groups, re-parent groups, assign-on-create) — see
[Implementation status](#implementation-status),
[Spending Chart](#spending-chart-graphical-presentation--built-),
[Drill-down](#drill-from-a-table-cell-into-the-expenses-view--built-), and
[Editable hierarchy](#editable-hierarchy--assign--re-parent--built-). Year-over-year
comparison (a table Change column + chart marker) is also built (see
[Year-over-year comparison](#year-over-year-comparison--table-columns--bar-marker-built-)).
Still deferred: selectable periods, richer YoY views (pace line / diverging),
tier CRUD, and export (see [Deferred](#deferred-later-slices)).

## Data model (new)

The category hierarchy today is flat: `categories (family_id, name, color)`.
There is no Grouping or Importance layer. v1 adds two tiers as real,
family-scoped tables so they are first-class and become editable later.

uploading receipt images, sometimes by typing the details in by hand — and the
app derives their expenses and reconciles them against imported bank activity.

**Family**:
The data-scoping unit. All Receipts, Transactions, Categories, and vendor rules
belong to a Family, and every access-control policy scopes to it. Each user gets
one solo Family auto-created at signup (`ensure_default_family()`); their
`is_default` Family is the one they operate on. A `families` row (`id`, `name`).
_Avoid_: household, account

**Family Member**:
A person who belongs to a Family — a `family_members` row (`family_id`,
`user_id`, `role`, `status`, `is_default`). `role ∈ {owner, member}` (the creator
is the `owner`; role is not yet used for authorization). `status ∈ {active,
invited, removed}`, but only `active` rows exist until Invitations ship. A member
is identified for display by their primary email (from `auth.users`), which the
client reads only through the `get_family_members()` `SECURITY DEFINER` RPC.
_Avoid_: user, member, participant

**Receipt**:
A record of a single purchase (merchant, amount, date). May originate from an
uploaded image or be entered by hand. Each Receipt maps to exactly one Expense.
_Avoid_: bill, purchase

**Manual Receipt**:
A Receipt a person creates by typing merchant, amount, and date rather than
uploading an image. It has no image and is not run through OCR; the person is
asserting the details — including the date — directly.
_Avoid_: manual entry, hand receipt

**Expense**:
The categorized view of a Receipt used for reporting. Derived one-to-one from a
Receipt — never stored on its own. Talk about Expenses when reporting or
categorizing; talk about Receipts when capturing.
_Avoid_: cost, spend

**Area of Importance**:
The top tier of the spending hierarchy — e.g. Essential, Priorities, Other. A
family-scoped `importance_areas` row with a `sort_order`. Attaches to the
**Grouping**, not to individual categories, so a Grouping has exactly one
Importance.
_Avoid_: priority band, tier

**Grouping**:
The middle tier of the spending hierarchy — e.g. Everyday, Home, Transportation.
A family-scoped `category_groups` row that belongs to one **Area of Importance**
and gathers many Categories. A Category with no Grouping is _Uncategorized_.
_Avoid_: group, bucket, section

**Spending Report**:
The categorized roll-up of a year's Expenses through Category → Grouping → Area
of Importance, shown as a month-by-month table (the `/spending` "Table" view) or
the **Spending Chart**. Replaces the family's hand-built spreadsheet pivot.
_Avoid_: pivot table, summary

**Spending Chart**:
The charted form of the **Spending Report**: stacked bars (one per Grouping,
stacked by month) with drilldown to Categories — the `/spending` "Chart" view.
_Avoid_: graph, dashboard

A line of activity imported from a bank or credit-card statement, reconciled
against Receipts. Distinct from a Receipt: it comes from the bank, not the user.
_Avoid_: charge, payment

**Split Receipt**:
A partial-amount Receipt carved off another. A split is a FULL Receipt record
(not a line-item or child), preserving the 1:1 Receipt↔Expense invariant so no
query or reconciliation code needs to change. Peers share a nullable, indexed
`split_group_id` (UUID). Created by an atomic insert-then-update — the new split
is inserted first, the original reduced second; if the update fails the split is
deleted (best-effort rollback). Both the original's and the split's
`matched_transaction_id` are cleared. Each split takes an optional per-split date
override (deferred charges: hotel/AirBnB/installments) and recomputes
`suspicious_date` from its own date. Splits share the original
`receipt_image_path` — no file is duplicated.
_Avoid_: line item, child receipt

the app, never an assertion. Always _potential_: a family can legitimately hold
two Receipts for the same merchant, amount and day. Duplicate-ness is a property
of a **pair** of Receipts, not of one Receipt, and it is derived on demand rather
than recorded. There is currently no way for a person to settle the suspicion.

**Family-scoped migration invariants**:
When categories and vendor rules moved from user- to family-scope, duplicates
were deduped keeping the FIRST-created row per key; the losing rows' receipt

(`unique_category_per_family` on `(family_id, LOWER(name))`); vendor patterns are
unique per `(family_id, vendor_pattern)`. Every family-scoped RLS policy requires

fix forward.

A Receipt's `total_amount` stays in its ORIGINAL currency; `exchange_rate_to_cad`
is stored on the Receipt at save time (fetched once, never during
reconciliation). Reconciliation matches CAD receipts within a $0.01 tolerance but

settlement timing all move the number. Rates come from the Bank of Canada Valet
API (series `FXEURCAD`, `FXUSDCAD`, `FXGBPCAD`).

`max(0, fileCount − dbCount)` rows, which makes re-import idempotent. The match

receipt edit modal is the confirmation action; there is no separate "confirm
date".

trustworthy stored fact and can be resolved globally with no such tension.

# The stored image is the contract

## Context & decision

`ReceiptService.uploadAndCreate()` validated the file the person picked and
_then_ shrank it. The 5MB limit therefore measured the **Source File** while the
resize that would have made it ~400KB ran on the next line. A modern phone photo
(3–5MB, or 8–12MB at 48MP) was rejected with "Image too large. Max 5MB." — the
app refusing to accept a file it was built to shrink, and asking the person to do
by hand the job the code does automatically. That is the failure that prompted
this ADR.

The fix is to decide what the limit is _about_. **The limit describes the
artifact we keep, not the artifact we are handed.** Size validation moves after
the resize, so it gates the **Receipt Image**; the Source File is bounded only by
a 25MB pre-decode ceiling that exists to protect the browser's memory, not to
judge the receipt. Everything follows from that principle:

- **2400px longest axis at 85% JPEG.** The stored image is what a person zooms
  into, so the pixel budget is chosen for human reading, not for OCR.
- **HEIC and PNG transcode to JPEG.** One stored format. PNG additionally never
  honoured the 85% quality argument (`toBlob` ignores it for lossless formats),
  so a PNG "resize" could return a file _larger_ than it arrived.
- **Zoom stops at the image's own natural resolution**, replacing a flat
  `MAX_ZOOM = 400`. 100% is fit-to-viewport, so a fixed percentage meant
  different things per device: on a phone 400% was roughly 1:1, on a desktop it
  demanded ~2.3× more detail than a 2000px file contains. The mush people saw at
  high zoom was the viewer promising pixels the resize had already discarded.
- **No backfill.** A per-image ceiling reads each generation correctly on its
  own. Re-resizing the pre-`901b670` full-resolution originals would destroy
  detail we already paid to store — so `/admin/resize-images` is deleted rather
  than updated, which also closes the **M2** finding (an unauthenticated
  delete-and-reupload page) instead of deferring it a fourth time.

## Considered options

- **Raise `MAX_IMAGE_MB` from 5 to ~15.** A one-line unblock, rejected because
  the gate would still measure the wrong artifact: a 16MB photo that resizes to
  400KB is still refused for no reason the family can perceive.
- **Keep the gate, improve the error message.** Cheapest, and the honest reading
  of it is "we have automated shrinking, and we are going to ask you to do it
  anyway."
- **Keep PNG lossless, add a keep-the-smaller-file guard.** Genuinely defensible
  — JPEG ringing around small glyphs is real, and screenshot receipts have sharp
  edges. Rejected for a single stored format; at 2400px and 85% the artefacts are
  well below the threshold that matters for reading a total.
- **Two artifacts per receipt** — a small display/OCR copy plus a large read
  copy. Best quality-per-byte, rejected as doubling the storage objects and
  adding a second signed-URL path to every surface that shows a receipt.
- **Cap zoom at ~1.5× native** rather than a hard 1:1, keeping some headroom
  because magnification past 1:1 still helps low-vision readers even though it
  adds no information. Rejected in favour of the stricter rule: every pixel on
  screen is a real pixel.

## Consequences

- **Transcoding is irreversible and lossy.** Detail discarded at upload never
  comes back — there is no original to re-derive from, by design. Revisiting the
  2400px/85% numbers only affects receipts uploaded after the change.
- **Zoom disappears for small images.** Anything already at or below viewport
  size has `MIN_ZOOM == MAX_ZOOM` and both controls sit disabled. Accepted
  deliberately over faking magnification.
- **A resize failure now becomes a rejection.** `prepareFileForUpload` falls back
  to the original on any error; a 12MB original then fails the post-resize gate.
  The file is refused either way, but the real reason is "we could not shrink
  it", and the message must say so rather than blaming the file's size.
- **The email path diverges.** The Resend handler uploads attachment bytes
  straight to storage with no size check and no resize (Deno — no Canvas), so an
  emailed receipt is stored full-size while the same receipt uploaded in the
  browser becomes 2400px JPEG. Resizing there needs a WASM image library and a
  second copy of these rules in `supabase/functions/_shared/`, kept in lock-step
  by hand. Logged in the [backlog](../product-backlog.md) rather than built.
- **Storage now holds three generations** of Receipt Image and always will. This
  is fine for zoom (see the "Zoom never invents pixels" invariant) but means
  storage-size statistics are not comparable across upload dates.

  copy. Best quality-per-byte, rejected as doubling the storage objects and
  adding a second signed-URL path to every surface that shows a receipt.
- **Cap zoom at ~1.5× native** rather than a hard 1:1, keeping some headroom
  because magnification past 1:1 still helps low-vision readers even though it
  adds no information. Rejected in favour of the stricter rule: every pixel on
  screen is a real pixel.

## Consequences

- **Transcoding is irreversible and lossy.** Detail discarded at upload never
  comes back — there is no original to re-derive from, by design. Revisiting the
  2400px/85% numbers only affects receipts uploaded after the change.
- **Zoom disappears for small images.** Anything already at or below viewport
  size has `MIN_ZOOM == MAX_ZOOM` and both controls sit disabled. Accepted
  deliberately over faking magnification.
- **A resize failure now becomes a rejection.** `prepareFileForUpload` falls back
  to the original on any error; a 12MB original then fails the post-resize gate.
  The file is refused either way, but the real reason is "we could not shrink
  it", and the message must say so rather than blaming the file's size.
- **The email path diverges.** The Resend handler uploads attachment bytes
  straight to storage with no size check and no resize (Deno — no Canvas), so an
  emailed receipt is stored full-size while the same receipt uploaded in the
  browser becomes 2400px JPEG. Resizing there needs a WASM image library and a
  second copy of these rules in `supabase/functions/_shared/`, kept in lock-step
  by hand. Logged in the [backlog](../product-backlog.md) rather than built.
- **Storage now holds three generations** of Receipt Image and always will. This
  is fine for zoom (see the "Zoom never invents pixels" invariant) but means
  storage-size statistics are not comparable across upload dates.

input.content: # Receipt Image Resize & Zoom Design **Date:** 2026-08-03 **Status:** 🟡 Designed, not built (pending release) Resize-on-upload and zoom both already ship (`901b670`). This is a correction to both, driven by a real failure: a phone photo was refused with "Image too large. Max 5MB." by the line immediately before the one that would have shrunk it to ~400KB. The governing decision — the size limit describes the **Receipt Image** we store, not the **Source File** we are handed — is recorded in [ADR-0006](../adr/0006-the-stored-image-is-the-contract.md), with the vocabulary and invariants in [the domain model](../domain-model.md). This document is the implementation shape. ## The defect ``` uploadAndCreate() ReceiptService.ts:186 ├─ validateFile(file) :187 ← rejects Source File > 5MB └─ withRetry( :190 prepareFileForUpload() :191 ← resize to 2000px / 85% uploadToStorage() :192 ``` `validateFile` (`:164`) reads `file.size` on the picked file. `MAX_IMAGE_MB = 5` (`:13`) is small next to a modern phone photo — 3–5MB typically, 8–12MB at 48MP — so the gate fires on files the pipeline exists to shrink. Nothing downstream rescues it. `FileValidator` (`src/lib/server/fileValidation.ts:13`, 10MB, magic-number based) is server-side and not on this path. The email-ingestion path (`supabase/functions/resend/handler.ts:137`) has no size check at all, so the same receipt forwarded by email is accepted at full size while the upload button refuses it. ## Changes ### 1. Validation splits in two `validateFile` currently answers one question with three checks. It becomes two gates around the resize: **Before decode** — file type against the allow-list, plus a **25MB** ceiling on any type. This ceiling is a memory guard, not a policy about receipts: it stops a 200MP panorama or a RAW export from hanging the tab before Canvas is even reached. Comfortably above a 48MP iPhone photo and a multi-page scanned PDF. **After resize** — the existing `MAX_IMAGE_MB` (5) / `MAX_PDF_MB` (10) applied to the file actually being uploaded. Note the shift in what a rejection _means_. `prepareFileForUpload` swallows any resize error and returns the original (`:215`), so a 12MB photo whose resize fails — Canvas OOM, a corrupt EXIF block, HEIC on a non-Apple browser — now falls back to a 12MB original that the second gate refuses. The file is refused either way, but the reason is "we could not shrink this", and the message must say that rather than repeating "too large", which would send the person off to do something that will not help. ### 2. Resize accepts HEIC and PNG, and always emits JPEG `resizeImage` returns early for anything that is not JPEG or PNG (`imageResize.ts:72`), while the upload control offers `image/heic` (`src/routes/receipts/+page.svelte:492`). Two independent problems follow from the format handling: - **HEIC is skipped entirely** — the backlog has flagged this as unverified on-device since the mobile-capture PRD. Safari (macOS/iOS) can decode HEIC into Canvas and Chrome/Firefox cannot, which is fortunate: HEIC only originates on Apple platforms. Feed it through the same path and fall back to the untouched original elsewhere. - **PNG is never compressed.** `canvas.toBlob(cb, file.type, quality)` (`:104`) ignores the quality argument for lossless formats, so 85% has never applied to a PNG. There is also no keep-the-smaller-file guard, so a sub-threshold PNG is re-encoded at identical dimensions and returned even when the result is bigger than what the person picked. Screenshots of e-receipts are usually PNG. Both dissolve if the output is always JPEG. `toBlob` is called with `'image/jpeg'` regardless of input, and the storage path extension follows. `original_filename` is unaffected and must stay that way — it deliberately captures the pre-resize name (`#{#ofn2a}`, `ReceiptService.ts:283`) so a receipt is listed under the name its owner recognizes, even though the stored object is now `.jpg`. **Consequential fix:** `extractReceiptDataFailSoft(path, file.type)` (`:193`) passes the _original_ file's MIME type while the object at `path` is the resized one. Harmless today; a live bug the moment HEIC transcodes, because OCR would be told `image/heic` about a JPEG. It must take the uploaded file's type. ### 3. Pixel budget: 2400px longest axis at 85% Up from 2000px, for headroom on receipts photographed at a distance, where the receipt occupies a fraction of the frame. Expected stored size ~500–800KB. The comment at `imageResize.ts:58` ("Images smaller than 2000px still have compression applied") is false for PNG today and should be corrected rather than carried forward. ### 4. Zoom stops at native resolution `ReceiptImageViewer.svelte` fits the image to the viewport at 100% (`handleImageLoad`, `:72`) and caps at a flat `MAX_ZOOM = 400` (`:56`). Those two constants were chosen independently and disagree: a 2400×1000 receipt on a 1440px-tall laptop fits at ~1150px, so 100% is ~48% of native and 400% asks the browser to paint ~4800px from a 2400px file. Everything past roughly 210% is interpolation. On a phone the same 400% lands near 1:1, so the current constant is approximately right there and badly wrong on a desktop. `MAX_ZOOM` becomes derived: `100 × naturalWidth / baseWidth`, the zoom at which one image pixel occupies one CSS pixel. `ZOOM_STEP` is 50 and `zoomIn`/`zoomOut` snap to multiples of it (`:127`, `:134`), so the derived ceiling will rarely be a multiple of 50 — the top step must clamp to the ceiling rather than skip past or become unreachable. Where the fit scale is already clamped at 1 (`:78`) — any image at or below viewport size — the ceiling equals `MIN_ZOOM` and both buttons sit permanently disabled. That is the accepted outcome, not an edge case to patch: there are no further real pixels, and the disabled control says so. It affects small PNGs and low-resolution receipts uploaded before resizing existed. ### 5. Delete `/admin/resize-images` A one-off migration page (~260 lines) whose job is finished. It would now do active harm — it re-resizes at its own hardcoded constants, permanently destroying the extra detail in pre-`901b670` full-resolution originals that the native-resolution zoom ceiling is designed to exploit. It is also the unauthenticated delete-and-reupload route recorded as **M2** in the [backlog](../product-backlog.md); deleting it closes the finding outright. Removing it also removes the second caller of `resizeImage`, so the new constants have exactly one call site. ### No backfill Storage will hold three generations of Receipt Image — full-resolution from before `901b670`, 2000px since, 2400px after this change. A ceiling derived from each image's own dimensions handles all three correctly with no migration; the older full-resolution receipts simply permit more zoom. ## What is deliberately not changing - **The email path.** `handler.ts:137` uploads attachment bytes straight to storage, unresized and ungated. It is a Deno edge function with no Canvas, so matching this behaviour means a WASM image library plus a second copy of the resize rules in `supabase/functions/_shared/`, kept in lock-step by hand — the same maintenance burden CLAUDE.md already flags for the date-correction code, and CPU time inside a webhook that must answer quickly. Logged as a backlog item instead. - **Resize inside `withRetry`.** Each retry re-decodes from the original (`:190`). Idempotent and correct — no cumulative recompression, since every attempt starts from the Source File — just mildly wasteful. Left alone. - **PDFs.** Stored as received, gated at 10MB, no zoom in the viewer (`isPdf`, delegated to the browser's PDF renderer). ## Memory `resizeImage` decodes the file twice: it builds an `` from an object URL purely to get an `onload` (`:77`, `:152`), then ignores that element and decodes the same bytes again via `createImageBitmap(file)` (`:89`). Peak memory is doubled on exactly the large files the 25MB ceiling now admits, and on an older phone that is the difference between working and a crashed tab. The `` is removable — `createImageBitmap` is itself the decode and needs no prior load event. This is a correctness prerequisite for raising the ceiling, not a tidy-up. In its favour: `processUploadBatch` (`src/lib/utils/batchUpload.ts:44`) is a sequential `for…of await`, so a multi-file selection never holds more than one decode at a time. ## Testing - `imageResize.spec.ts` — dimension maths at the new 2400px threshold; HEIC and PNG both produce `image/jpeg`; output is never larger than the input. - `ReceiptService` specs — a Source File over 5MB but under 25MB now succeeds (the reported failure, as a regression test); over 25MB is refused before decode; a resize failure on a large file is refused with the shrink-failure message; the MIME passed to OCR matches the uploaded file, not the picked one. - `ReceiptImageViewer.svelte.spec.ts` — ceiling derived from natural size; controls disabled when natural ≤ viewport; top step clamps to the ceiling rather than overshooting. - Manual, on-device: an iPhone upload end-to-end, plus the gesture check already standing in the backlog (wheel/drag/pinch after the a11y action refactor). ## Open questions 1. **Does 2400px buy OCR anything?** Mistral's vision model downscales large inputs internally; if its effective ceiling is ~1024–1500px on an axis, the extra pixels serve human zoom only. Worth confirming against Mistral's docs — it does not change the decision, but it changes the rationale, and it would let a future storage squeeze cut resolution without touching OCR accuracy. 2. **What does an iPhone actually hand over?** Still unverified on-device. The transcode is designed to work whether Safari offers HEIC or converts to JPEG itself, so this is validation rather than a blocker.

content.content:
## Engineering

### In progress

- **🟢 Bombadil property-based UI testing (spike) — built and running.** `bombadil/transactions.ts` explores `/transactions` against the local stack with 12 properties (the 4 free ones plus a pathname tripwire, filter/counter/selection invariants). Session comes from a DEV-and-loopback-gated auto-login (`src/lib/dev/autoLogin.ts`); `npm run bombadil` after `npm run db:fresh` + `npm run dev`. A clean 60-second run explores ~390 actions (≈5/sec) with no violations. Open follow-ups: **`PressKey` wedges the run** — every run including it hung with the browser at 100% CPU, so keyboard interaction is excluded entirely and the cause is undiagnosed; **native `<select>` popups hang it too**, so the card/bank-type filter is unexplored (Chrome renders the option list outside the page); **Delete / bulk-delete are excluded** because they use `confirm()`; and **`--reproduce` has never been exercised**. Widening to a second page (which means a second hand-written specification, not a config change) and deciding whether it earns a nightly GitHub Action (`antithesishq/bombadil-action@v2`) are the next questions. See [Bombadil spike handoff](plans-done/2026-07-26-bombadil-property-testing-spike.md).

### Security

- **🟠 HIGH — unverified, non-unique profile emails allow email-ingestion hijack.** _(Found 2026-07-17 audit; the top open security item.)_ The add-email flow (`src/routes/profile/+page.svelte`) lets a user attach ANY address to their profile (`profiles.email_1..5`) with only format + within-own-profile dedup — **no ownership verification and no cross-user unique constraint**. The Resend webhook attributes inbound receipts via `find_user_by_email(sender)`, which falls through to those profile columns (`resend/handler.ts`). So an attacker can claim a victim's forwarding/secondary address and have the victim's forwarded receipts ingested into the attacker's account (data leak), or make attribution nondeterministic (`limit 1`) when two profiles claim the same address, or pre-claim an address to poison a future user. Not closed by the webhook-signature fix — the abuse is by a legitimately authed user. Fix: confirm ownership via emailed token before an alias participates in lookup; add a global `UNIQUE(lower(email))` (ideally a normalized `profile_emails` table); prefer exact `auth.users` identity over unverified aliases.
- **Sweep the remaining `SECURITY DEFINER` functions for missing `anon` revokes.** The seed-function lockdown found that `REVOKE … FROM PUBLIC` left a _direct_ `anon` grant in place, needing an explicit `REVOKE … FROM anon`. Only `create_default_hierarchy` / `create_default_categories` were fixed that way. Audit every other `SECURITY DEFINER` function for the same hole and revoke explicitly where `authenticated` is the only legitimate caller.
- **🟢 LOW / deferred audit items (re-verified 2026-07-17).** Unchanged since the 2026-07-05 audit — see the [Security Remediation PRD "Deferred" section](prd-done/prd-security-remediation.md): **H3** `/api/ocr` + `/api/ocr/extract` are unauthenticated and SSRF-able via a caller-supplied `fileUrl` (no auth, no host allow-list — `src/routes/api/ocr/**`); **M1** the Resend webhook still logs full request headers (`resend/handler.ts:334`, including svix signature material) and an API-key prefix/suffix (`:389`); **M2** `/admin/resize-images` is a client-only page that deletes and re-uploads receipt originals with no authz beyond `confirm()`; **M3** the `families` INSERT policy is `WITH CHECK (auth.uid() IS NOT NULL)` only (no `created_by` binding, no limit); **F6** `email_send_failures` SELECT is whole-family-scoped, so co-members can read each other's notification recipient + subject — confirm that's intended.

### Dependencies

- **High vuln: `xlsx` (SheetJS) has no npm fix — decision needed.** `npm audit` reports 1 high against `xlsx@^0.18.5` — Prototype Pollution ([GHSA-4r6h-8v6p-xvw6](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4r6h-8v6p-xvw6), fixed in 0.19.3) and ReDoS ([GHSA-5pgg-2g8v-p4x9](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5pgg-2g8v-p4x9), fixed in 0.20.2). Both fixes exist **only on the SheetJS CDN (`cdn.sheetjs.com`), not npm** — the npm package is unmaintained, so `npm audit` will never clear and there is no version to bump to. Used only by the Excel importer, contained in `src/lib/services/ExcelToCSVConverter.ts` behind a stable interface; the app supports **both** legacy `.xls` (BIFF8) and `.xlsx`. Options: (a) pin the CDN tarball via `overrides` — clears the CVEs and keeps `.xls`, but adds a non-registry dep our `min-release-age` hardening can't gate; (b) migrate to `exceljs` — maintained, but **cannot read legacy `.xls`**, so it drops that support unless paired with a BIFF parser. **The decision to make: is legacy `.xls` still required?** Deferred — the importer is not internet-exposed (users upload their own bank exports), which lowers practical risk.
- **Low vulns: `cookie` (via `@sveltejs/kit`) and `esbuild` dev server.** (1) `cookie <0.7.0` accepts out-of-bounds characters in name/path/domain ([GHSA-pxg6-pf52-xh8x](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pxg6-pf52-xh8x)), pulled in transitively through `@sveltejs/kit` → `@sveltejs/adapter-auto` / `runed` / `layerchart`; `npm audit fix --force` would downgrade `@sveltejs/kit` to `1.0.0-next.0` (breaking), so wait for the framework chain to bump `cookie`. (2) `esbuild 0.27.3–0.28.0` allows arbitrary file read when the dev server runs on Windows ([GHSA-g7r4-m6w7-qqqr](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g7r4-m6w7-qqqr)) — dev-only, non-Windows here; clearable with a plain `npm audit fix`. Low priority; both are dev/transitive, not shipped to users.
- **🔴 New since the last audit: 6 further `npm audit` findings, 2 of them critical.** _(Surfaced 2026-07-26 while adding the Bombadil dev dependency; none introduced by it — `@antithesishq/bombadil` has zero dependencies. The total is now 9: 2 low, 1 moderate, 4 high, 2 critical.)_ Every one claims a fix via a plain `npm audit fix`, so this is mostly a bump-and-verify job — but it needs the fixes actually applied and the suites re-run, not just logged.
  - **CRITICAL — `@vitest/browser <=3.2.6`:** Browser Mode provider commands bypass the file-access permission gate ([GHSA-p63j-vcc4-9vmv](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p63j-vcc4-9vmv)). Two advisories, counted against both `@vitest/browser` and `vitest`. We run browser-mode tests, so this is the one to fix first.
  - **MODERATE — `@sveltejs/kit <=2.70.1`:** prototype pollution in the remote-function form file-input deletion path ([GHSA-866w-xmhq-wj7x](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-866w-xmhq-wj7x)), plus a Node crash on large remote-form payloads ([GHSA-wqjv-9729-c5q2](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wqjv-9729-c5q2)). We don't use remote functions today, but this is shipped framework code.
  - **HIGH — `postcss <=8.5.17`:** path traversal via `sourceMappingURL` auto-loading discloses arbitrary `.map` files ([GHSA-r28c-9q8g-f849](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r28c-9q8g-f849)).
  - **HIGH — `js-yaml 4.0.0–4.2.0`:** merge-key chains force quadratic CPU ([GHSA-52cp-r559-cp3m](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-52cp-r559-cp3m)). Build-time only.

Session comes from a DEV-and-loopback-gated auto-login (`src/lib/dev/autoLogin.ts`); `npm run bombadil` after `npm run db:fresh` + `npm run dev`. A clean 60-second run explores ~390 actions (≈5/sec) with no violations. Open follow-ups: **`PressKey` wedges the run** — every run including it hung with the browser at 100% CPU, so keyboard interaction is excluded entirely and the cause is undiagnosed; **native `<select>` popups hang it too**, so the card/bank-type filter is unexplored (Chrome renders the option list outside the page); **Delete / bulk-delete are excluded** because they use `confirm()`; and **`--reproduce` has never been exercised**. - **🟠 HIGH — unverified, non-unique profile emails allow email-ingestion hijack.** _(Found 2026-07-17 audit; the top open security item.)_ The add-email flow (`src/routes/profile/+page.svelte`) lets a user attach ANY address to their profile (`profiles.email_1..5`) with only format + within-own-profile dedup — **no ownership verification and no cross-user unique constraint**. The Resend webhook attributes inbound receipts via `find_user_by_email(sender)`, which falls through to those profile columns (`resend/handler.ts`). So an attacker can claim a victim's forwarding/secondary address and have the victim's forwarded receipts ingested into the attacker's account (data leak), or make attribution nondeterministic (`limit 1`) when two profiles claim the same address, or pre-claim an address to poison a future user. Fix: confirm ownership via emailed token before an alias participates in lookup; add a global `UNIQUE(lower(email))` (ideally a normalized `profile_emails` table); prefer exact `auth.users` identity over unverified aliases.
